subtopic_detail: Progressive magnetic gait with urinary urgency and mild cognitive slowing alongside ventriculomegaly on imaging
stem: A 76-year-old man has 18 months of unsteadiness with three falls, slowing of thought, and urinary urgency with two episodes of incontinence.

data_table.Examination: Broad based shuffling gait with difficulty initiating; no tremor or rigidity; MoCA 24 out of 30
data_table.Imaging: MRI brain enlarged lateral ventricles with Evans index 0.37 and a narrowed callosal angle

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly for ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion
options.rationale: Shunting is the definitive treatment but carries risks of infection, subdural haematoma and overdrainage, so patient selection rests on demonstrating that cerebrospinal fluid removal actually improves gait rather than on imaging appearances alone. Imaging findings like these are also seen in people who do not respond to shunting. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.text: Trial levodopa with carbidopa and reassess the gait at four weeks
options.rationale: A levodopa trial is used when the picture suggests parkinsonism, which typically brings asymmetric bradykinesia, rigidity with cogwheeling, reduced arm swing and a resting tremor, none of which he has. Gait apraxia with preserved arm swing and normal tone points elsewhere. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Large volume lumbar puncture with timed gait testing before and after
options.rationale: Removing thirty to fifty millilitres of cerebrospinal fluid and formally measuring gait speed and a timed walk before and several hours after is the standard test of whether this gait will respond to shunting, and a clear improvement predicts benefit. It also excludes raised opening pressure and allows cerebrospinal fluid analysis for alternative causes. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor and review cognition in three months
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors treat Alzheimer disease and dementia with Lewy bodies and have no role in a potentially reversible hydrocephalic picture, and his cognitive deficits are executive rather than amnestic. Starting one here would delay a treatable diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Urodynamic studies and an antimuscarinic for the urinary urgency
options.rationale: Treating the bladder in isolation ignores the unifying explanation for gait, cognition and continence, and antimuscarinics worsen cognition in older adults. Urinary symptoms in this syndrome improve when the underlying problem is treated. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a potentially reversible cause of gait disturbance in older people, characterised by the triad of a magnetic apraxic gait, urinary urgency and incontinence, and subcortical cognitive slowing, with gait usually the earliest and most shunt responsive feature. Imaging shows ventriculomegaly disproportionate to cortical atrophy, commonly quantified by an Evans index above 0.3, with a narrowed callosal angle and crowded sulci at the high convexity. Because ventricular enlargement also accompanies cerebral atrophy and other neurodegenerative disease, imaging alone cannot select patients for surgery, and a supplementary test of cerebrospinal fluid removal is used: a large volume lumbar puncture with objective gait measurement before and after, or extended external lumbar drainage in equivocal cases. Patients who improve after fluid removal have substantially higher rates of benefit from ventriculoperitoneal shunting, with gait improving most reliably and cognition least. The main differentials are vascular parkinsonism, Parkinson disease, and cervical myelopathy, and the practical error is attributing a treatable gait disorder to age or to dementia.
key_points: Gait disturbance is the earliest and most shunt responsive element of the triad.
Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, with a narrowed callosal angle, supports the diagnosis.
Imaging cannot select surgical candidates, so a cerebrospinal fluid removal test is performed.
Objective timed gait measurement before and after the tap is what makes the test interpretable.
Preserved arm swing with normal tone argues against Parkinson disease as the cause.
explanation.pearls: Measure the gait formally with a timed ten metre walk and a timed up and go before the tap and again three to four hours afterwards, because subjective impressions from the patient and family after a lumbar puncture are unreliable and a documented improvement of around twenty per cent is what drives the neurosurgical referral.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on normal pressure hydrocephalus

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice in acute pyelonephritis requiring admission
stem:
You are the emergency registrar admitting a 34 year old woman with 24 hours of fever, rigors and right loin pain. She has vomited three times this morning and cannot keep down oral fluids.

She is not pregnant on a beta human chorionic gonadotrophin test, and has had no urinary catheter, hospitalisation or antibiotic exposure in the last six months. She has no known drug allergies and takes no regular medication. She has right renal angle tenderness on examination. Her urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes and a specimen has gone for culture. Her creatinine and potassium are within normal limits and a bedside ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 104/64, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.1
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick nitrites and leucocytes positive; urine culture pending; bedside ultrasound no hydronephrosis
data_table.Blood tests: White cell count 16.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); creatinine and potassium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for fourteen days with early general practitioner review
options.rationale: She is vomiting and cannot absorb oral therapy, and trimethoprim resistance rates in Australian urinary isolates are too high for empirical use in systemic infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for seven days with oral rehydration in the department
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin is the classic near pair error here because it concentrates in urine but does not achieve therapeutic renal parenchymal or serum levels, so it never treats pyelonephritis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for seven days once the vomiting has been controlled
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved in Australia for resistant isolates or specific allergy situations because of resistance stewardship and tendinopathy and neuropathy risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin with a loading dose calculated on actual body weight and level monitoring
options.rationale: Vancomycin covers Gram positive organisms and misses the Gram negative Enterobacterales that cause the overwhelming majority of pyelonephritis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin with intravenous amoxicillin and review at 48 hours with the culture
options.rationale: Australian empirical therapy for pyelonephritis requiring admission is intravenous gentamicin plus amoxicillin, covering Enterobacterales and enterococci, with narrowing once susceptibilities return (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis is distinguished from lower urinary tract infection by systemic features such as fever, rigors and loin pain, and this distinction determines both the antibiotic and its route. Agents that concentrate in urine without achieving tissue levels, notably nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin, are effective for cystitis and useless for upper tract disease. Australian empirical therapy uses gentamicin with amoxicillin, with a single daily gentamicin dose and level monitoring if therapy continues beyond 48 hours. Imaging is reserved for those failing to improve at 48 to 72 hours, for suspected obstruction, or for a known stone history, since obstruction with infection is a urological emergency.
key_points: Fever, rigors and loin pain define upper tract infection and change the drug and the route
Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin never treat pyelonephritis despite good urinary concentrations
Empirical Australian therapy is intravenous gentamicin plus amoxicillin
Reimage at 48 to 72 hours if there is no clinical improvement
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin in this setting is given as a single daily dose of 4 to 7 mg/kg using ideal body weight, and a trough level is only required if therapy extends beyond 48 hours or renal function is impaired.
